title: Test: Multi-Agent Coordination
summary: Check what you learned across the whole chapter.

questions.q: The section **Optimistic Concurrency Control** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: An all-results barrier meets a deadline with probability F(t)^N, and a k-of-N rule recovers most of it only when results are interchangeable.

Shared working directories produce lost updates and torn reads, and write sets collide with probability 1 - exp(-N(N-1)w^2/2F), so isolation is provided per worker and a merge is validated, not trusted.
Dynamic spawning makes the execution graph nondeterministic, so the runtime enforces fan-out, concurrency, depth, and deadline bounds and reserves each child's maximum liability before it starts.
The dependency graph, the communication topology, and the supervision tree are separate structures, and conflating them hides quadratic communication cost and orphaned lifecycles.

questions.q: The section **Fallacies and Pitfalls** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Cancellation scope follows delegation lineage and closes admission at each gate, but cancelling a subtree does not settle the obligations its admitted work already created.
The runtime assigns each child an identity and a grant contained in its delegator's, sharing permissions but partitioning consumable allowances by atomic reservation.

With a fixed slot pool, a dependency graph's completion time is bounded below by both its critical path and its total slot work divided by the slots.

questions.q: True or false: in the book's concept map, *Coordination overhead* adds coordination cost to *Trajectory as the unit of engineering*.
questions.hint: Which later concept does this idea actually connect to?
questions.explanation: False. The book links *Coordination overhead* adds coordination cost to *Critical-path acceleration ceiling*.

questions.q: The section **The Delegation Trade-Off** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A credit window enforces free plus outstanding equal to W, bounding in-flight payload and, by Little's law, mean staleness at W/mu, which per-agent token budgets cannot do.

Shared working directories produce lost updates and torn reads, and write sets collide with probability 1 - exp(-N(N-1)w^2/2F), so isolation is provided per worker and a merge is validated, not trusted.

For a fixed amount of work with no coordination overhead, the serial fraction 1-p caps speedup at 1/(1-p) however many workers are added, and the universal scalability law reduces to it when coherency is zero.
Under Speedup(N) = 1/((1-p) + p/N + c(N)) any gain requires c(N) < p(1 - 1/N), the best count sits near sqrt(p/c) for linear overhead, and the serial fraction caps speedup at 1/(1-p).
